subtitle: Foreign words, Latin phrases and consultant German
words.intro: Educated German has always had a taste for a foreign word. Latin came first, then French, and today it’s English. A consultant can say an entire sentence in which only *der* and *und* are German. This chapter is your protection.

grammar[0].fact: *Sensibel* is one of the worst traps there is: it means sensitive. If you tell a German boss that you’re *sensibel*, you’ve said you cry easily. *Eventuell* likewise means perhaps. And *bekommen* doesn’t mean become, as you have known since A1.

grammar[1].blocks[2].text: If you don’t understand a word, say so: *Was heißt das konkret?* It’s not rude, it’s not a sign of bad German, and nine others in the room have been waiting for someone to ask.
grammar[1].fact: German has a long tradition of fighting foreign words. In the 17th century language societies invented *Briefwechsel* and *Leidenschaft*, and those stuck. They are also said to have tried *Gesichtserker*, “face bay window”, for the nose. That one, happily, did not.

reading.intro: The property company has paid a consultant, Herr Dr. Vogt, to “optimise” the house at Hofstraße 12. He has called a meeting of the tenants. There are biscuits. He has slides. Frau Huber has come with notebook number 18. Max is supposed to translate.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der Bildschirm: Das nehmen wir offline.
reading.fact: Many German words that look English aren’t: *das Handy*, *der Beamer*, *das Home-Office*, and you won’t be understood in London. And false friends aren’t only English: *eventuell* means *perhaps*, and *aktuell* means *current*. It’s easy to agree to something *eventually* that you meant only as a possibility.
